name: Afrikaans
confidence_why: Donaldson (1993) gives first-syllable stress for words of Germanic origin, but the specialist work on Afrikaans stress (Wissing 1989, 2019, 2020), including an acoustic corpus study, puts main stress at the right edge of monomorphemic words (final unless that syllable is unstressable, then penultimate) with initial stress only in compounds, so the fixed: initial syllable coding holds for native simplexes and compounds but not as the word-stress system.
catalog_quote: In words of Germanic origin the stress is on the first syllable although there are many exceptions to this in certain derived forms
sweep_summary: The title search produced one item for Afrikaans, Venter 1978 'Word stress in the English of Afrikaans-speaking undergraduates' (English usage in southern Africa 9(2): 15-18, Glottolog 43035 from Maho's eballiso2009): it is about L2 English word stress, not Afrikaans; no online copy or Crossref record exists; priority none. The catalog record (fixed-strict initial, domain word, deciding text Donaldson 1993:27 §1.10.1, cite field empty) is contradicted by the dedicated Afrikaans stress literature already held held by the project from the 16 Sep check pass and re-read now: Wissing 2020 JIPA 50(1):137 ('Primary stress lies predominantly on the final syllable of monomorphemic words, unless such a syllable is unstressable.. when penultimate or antepenultimate stress is required'), Wissing 2019 LitNet Akademies 16(2):214/219 (HKR: penult when the final syllable is unstressable, else final when strong; typing Afrikaans as an initial-stress language is 'onvanpas'), Taalportaal 2020 MSR (same rule; notes Lee 1963, De Villiers 1965, Combrink & De Stadler 1987 as the initial/free-stress minority) and Wissing 1989 Literator 10(2):58 rule (9). Best new statement: Wissing 2020 JIPA p. 137, which supersedes Donaldson as the deciding source; recommended reclassify as weight/stressability-hedged right-edge (as dutc1256), keeping Donaldson 1993:27 for the native-Germanic simplex/compound stratum. Still unread and paywalled at Taylor & Francis (not reachable by automated download; Crossref metadata saved): Wissing 1991 SAJL 9(2):47-57 'Is Afrikaans 'n inisiëleklemtoontaal?' plus the De Stadler 1991 and Lubbe 1993 replies and Wissing 1988 'ABRAKADABRA' (medium priority, would document the debate); Wissing 2007 SALALS acoustic correlates (low).

new_statements.quote: Primary stress lies predominantly on the final syllable of monomorphemic words, unless such a syllable is unstressable (usually with schwa as nucleus) when penultimate or antepenultimate stress is required. ... Words ending on /ɑ/, illustrate a strong tendency towards penultimate stress, irrespective of the word length ... [pɑˈtɑtɑ] patatta ... [jɑkɑˈrɑndɑ] jakaranda ... Final syllables in words of Classic origin generally carry primary stress ... In compounds, it is normally the first constituent that receives primary stress, whereas secondary stress will be on the second constituent ... Prefixes and suffixes in words of Germanic origin are normally not stressed ... [bəˈxən] begin, [xəˈnaːdə] genade, [fərˈbaːs] verbaas ... Non-native suffixes (or pseudo-suffixes) normally do carry primary stress
new_statements.citation: Wissing, Daan P. 2020. Afrikaans (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(1): 127-140. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000269
new_statements.reading: The field's specialist, in the peer-reviewed JIPA Illustration, states a right-edge, stressability-conditioned main stress rule for Afrikaans monomorphemes (final unless the final syllable is unstressable/schwa, then penult or antepenult; words in -a penult; Classical-origin words final), with initial stress only as the compound rule and Germanic affixes unstressed. This is the same class as the catalog's Dutch record (weight/stressability-hedged right-edge), not fixed-strict initial. Donaldson 1993:27 remains a correct statement for non-derived native Germanic simplexes and compounds, but its own scope restriction ('words of Germanic origin', 'many exceptions.. in derived forms') already denies word-domain strictness. Wissing 2019 (LitNet, corpus-acoustic) and Taalportaal 2020 say the same in Afrikaans and English respectively.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress lies on 1) the penultimate syllable of monomorphemic words ending on an unstressable syllable, or 2) on the antepenultimate syllable when followed by more than one unstressable syllables, except 3) when other factors dictate final stress. A possible rephrasing of this rule is: Primary stress lies on the final syllable of a monomorpheme, unless such syllable is unstressable, when penultimate or antepenultimate stress is required. [...] The MSR basically states that either the final or else the penultimate syllable of monomorphemes carries primary stress [...]. While Afrikaans is a Germanic language, some phonologists describe Afrikaans as an initial stress language, like Ancient Germanic (notably Lee 1963 and De Villiers 1965).

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's StressTyp2 record (initial stress = fixed initial): Wissing's Main Stress Rule is a right-edge, stressability-conditioned rule (final unless unstressable, then penult/antepenult), and he explicitly names the initial-stress view (Lee 1963, De Villiers 1965) as a competing older analysis. Agrees with and refines the existing Wissing 2020 JIPA statement (same author, same rule), adding the exception classes (pseudo-compounds, proper names, unique lexical exceptions) and the diachronic drift toward final stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In monomorphemes, primary stress is on the final syllable unless that syllable is unstressable (schwa or a short vowel in an open syllable), in which case stress goes to the penult, or to the antepenult when more than one unstressable syllable follows. Final closed syllables, long vowels and diphthongs attract final stress; short vowels in open final syllables are unstressed (words in -a have penultimate stress irrespective of length, e.g. jakaranda, abrakadabra); final /i/ in French-origin words (anatomie, energie) is stressed. Initial stress is the compound pattern, found in monomorphemes only in pseudo-compounds (eekhoring, ooievaar, seekoei, aalwyn) and Germanic proper names (Albert, Hoffman).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed on these pages (the Afrikaans Taalportaal word-stress module lists only primary-stress topics; secondary stress appears only in the Dutch menu).
new_statements.exceptions: Exceptions page: (1) pseudo-compounds with compound (initial) stress: aalwyn, aambei, aarbei, asfalt, biskop, eiland, eekhoring, eland, hertog, kinkhoes, koevoet, ooievaar, piekniek, seekoei, skeurbuik, etc; (2) Germanic proper names with initial stress (Albert, Ferdinand, Rudolf; Bergmann, Hoffman, Schoeman); place names in -burg/-dal/-dorp/-rand/-vlei shifting to final-member stress (Ventersdorp); (3) unique lexical exceptions, mostly 3+ syllables: alfabet, alkohol, altaar, karnaval, three of which are now shifting stress rightward. Overview page: words in -ies (basies, krities) have penult not final stress; amen/eksamen/tentamen unstressed final /ɛ/; kwaliteit often initial-stressed in informal speech; 'by far the most exceptions' are in words ending on short vowels. Stress-shift page: a strong tendency for originally initial-stressed multisyllabic monomorphemes to shift stress to the final syllable (akkusatief, almanak, karnaval, majesteit, medikus, uniform..), some still in flux; handhaaf/waarsku final stress 'mostly heard in coloured Afrikaans'.
new_statements.identity_note: Taalportaal describes standard (white) Afrikaans monomorphemes; the Stress-shift page notes that final stress in handhaaf and waarsku is 'mostly heard in coloured Afrikaans', the only variety remark found. De Boer 1999 describes no natural language variety (simulated vowel systems).

new_statements.quote: De Stadler is van mening dat Afrikaans 'n inisiëleklemtoontaal is. Hy kritiseer nie net die hoofklemtoonreël van Wissing, wat die klemtoon basies op die voorfinale of die finale sillabe plaas nie [...] Die algemene gevolgtrekking waartoe ge-kom is, is dat die Wissing-reël op beskrywende en voorspellende vlak meer doeltreffend is as die klemtoonreël van De Stadler, en dat daar goeie grond is waarop Afrikaans nie as inisiëleklemtoontaal getipeer kan word nie.
new_statements.translation: De Stadler holds that Afrikaans is an initial-stress language. He criticises not only Wissing's main stress rule, which places the stress basically on the penultimate or the final syllable [...] The general conclusion reached is that the Wissing rule is more effective than De Stadler's stress rule at the descriptive and predictive level, and that there are good grounds on which Afrikaans cannot be typed as an initial-stress language.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Afrikaans fixed-strict initial (StressTyp2, Donaldson 1993:27 'words of Germanic origin.. first syllable'). Wissing 1991 (abstract) states a penult-or-final main stress rule and concludes Afrikaans cannot be typed as an initial-stress language: a different edge and type. It agrees with the existing statements held by the project from Wissing 1989, 2019, 2020 (JIPA) and Taalportaal 2020 (right-edge, stressability-conditioned). Only the abstract was readable; the deciding sentences of the article body (pp. 47-57) remain unread.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the abstract: Wissing's main stress rule for Afrikaans simplexes puts primary stress basically on the penultimate or the final syllable (right edge), supported by ordinary simplexes, place names and letter/numeral names; the article argues explicitly that Afrikaans should NOT be classified as an initial-stress language (contra De Stadler). The conditioning between final and penult (unstressable/schwa final syllable -> penult) is stated in Wissing's other, already-read works (1989 Literator rule (9); 2020 JIPA; Taalportaal), not in the abstract itself.
new_statements.exceptions: abstract says the Wissing rule handles place names and letter- and numeral-names as well as ordinary simplexes; no exception list visible
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Afrikaans simplexes (monomorphemic words), including place names and letter/numeral names, per the abstract; no dialect restriction stated.

tone_statements.citation: Pfiffner, Alexandra M. 2025. Women of All Ages Lead Tonogenesis in Afrikaans. Journal of Germanic Linguistics 37(3): 270-286. doi:10.1017/S1470542725100056
tone_statements.quote: Coetzee et al. (2014, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 135, 2421), however, showed that the voicing contrast is collapsing word-initially, with voiced plosives merging with voiceless plosives. They also found that voicing loss does not result in loss of lexical contrast, which is preserved on the following vowel (high f0 after historically voiceless and low f0 after historically voiced plosives). … While lexical contrasts are hence cued by only f0 word initially, they are differentiated by both plosive voicing and the f0 of the following vowel word medially.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3106, meeting abstract (sole paragraph, sentences 2-3 and 9)
tone_statements.summary: Incipient position-restricted pitch contrast: word-initially high vs low f0 after historically voiceless vs voiced plosives is the sole cue to the lexical contrast; medially voicing and f0 both cue.

tone_statements.citation: Pfiffner, Alexandra M. 2021. Cue-based features: Modeling change and variation in the voicing contrasts of Minnesotan English, Afrikaans, and Dutch. PhD dissertation, Georgetown University.
tone_statements.quote: Afrikaans is undergoing tonogenesis as word-initial [voice] contrasts are neutralizing. A previous study by Coetzee and colleagues (2018) with all-female participants found: … • All participants produce large f0 differences in the following vowel to signal underlying voicing … • In the absence of prevoicing, f0 is a cue for phonological voicing for all listener/speaker demographic combinations, but less so for the perception of male speakers … [voice] cue weights are not changing uniformly as Afrikaans undergoes tonogenesis.
tone_statements.locator: Poster p. 1, panels 'Overview' (opening sentence and bullets), 'Discussion' (last bullet) and 'Conclusion' (first sentence)
tone_statements.summary: Incipient, positionally restricted pitch contrast: f0 of the vowel after a word-initial plosive cues the eroding /b,d/ vs /p,t/ voicing contrast (tonogenesis in progress); no tone inventory is given.

tone_statements.citation: Coetzee, Andries W., Patrice S. Beddor & Daan P. Wissing. 2014. Emergent tonogenesis in Afrikaans. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 135(4, Supplement): 2421-2422 (167th ASA Meeting abstract). doi:10.1121/1.4878043
tone_statements.quote: Word-initial plosives in Afrikaans are undergoing voicing neutralization; what was previously prevoiced /b, d/ is frequently produced as voiceless unaspirated [p, t] (Coetzee et al. 2018). [...] the phonetic cues to obstruent voicing are allowing tone to emerge in a process of tonogenesis, where phonological tone arises in a previously non-tonal language (Hombert 1975). [...] What was a historical obstruent voicing contrast is now variably produced, and with a strengthened f0 cue; this suggests that this is a case of tonogenesis, where the secondary f0 cues of the original obstruent voicing contrast are being rephonologized as tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 270, section 1 Introduction and p. 284, section 5 Conclusion

readall_conflicts: The catalog's StressTyp2 record for Afrikaans (fixed initial, initial stress) is contradicted by every Wissing source now obtained by the project: the Taalportaal Main Stress Rule (final unless the final syllable is unstressable, then penult/antepenult), the JIPA 2020 Illustration already in existing_statements, and Wissing 2019 (LitNet). Wissing himself notes the disagreement inside the field: Lee 1963 and De Villiers 1965 describe Afrikaans as an initial-stress language, and Combrink and De Stadler 1987 call it a free-stress language whose rules run from the left edge; Wissing 1991 (not obtainable here) is the paper that argued against the initial-stress analysis, and De Stadler 1991 and Lubbe 1993 replied. The initial-stress picture holds for compounds, pseudo-compounds and Germanic proper names, which is what the older analyses and Donaldson 1993 generalised from. The catalog codes Afrikaans as fixed-strict initial stress (StressTyp2; Donaldson 1993:27, itself scoped to 'words of Germanic origin' with 'many exceptions'). Wissing 1991, readable here only through the publisher's abstract on the NISC page, states that his main stress rule places stress 'basies op die voorfinale of die finale sillabe' and concludes 'dat daar goeie grond is waarop Afrikaans nie as inisiëleklemtoontaal getipeer kan word nie' - a right-edge (penult/final) rule and an explicit rejection of the initial-stress typing, i.e. it contradicts the catalog record and agrees with the statements already he…

audit.recode_to: weight-hedged (right-edge: final if final syllable heavy/stressable, else penult, antepenult when two unstressable syllables follow; schwa unstressable; lexical exceptions; Germanic prefixes unstressed, compound stress initial) — i.e. the same class as the Dutch record dutc1256; cite Wissing 2020 JIPA 50(1):137 and Taalportaal MSR, keep Donaldson 1993:27 as the Germanic-stratum/compound statement. At minimum drop counts as exceptionless (the strict set): Donaldson's own pp. 27-33 list systematic non-initial stress (be-/ge-/ver-/ont- verbs, -es/-in/-y/-ery, ~60 stressed loan endings).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Donaldson 1993 sentence is verbatim in the djvu text we hold at p. 27 section 1.10.1 (lines 2576-2586). sources.quote: Coetzee et al. (2014, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 135, 2421), however, showed that the voicing contrast is collapsing word-initially, with voiced plosives merging with voiceless plosives. They also found that voicing loss does not result in loss of lexical contrast, which is preserved on the following vowel (high f0 after historically voiceless and low f0 after historically voiced plosives). … While lexical contrasts are hence cued by only f0 word initially, they are differentiated by both plosive voicing and the f0 of the following vowel word medially.

sources.quote: Afrikaans is undergoing tonogenesis as word-initial [voice] contrasts are neutralizing. A previous study by Coetzee and colleagues (2018) with all-female participants found: … • All participants produce large f0 differences in the following vowel to signal underlying voicing … • In the absence of prevoicing, f0 is a cue for phonological voicing for all listener/speaker demographic combinations, but less so for the perception of male speakers … [voice] cue weights are not changing uniformly as Afrikaans undergoes tonogenesis.

sources.quote: Word-initial plosives in Afrikaans are undergoing voicing neutralization; what was previously prevoiced /b, d/ is frequently produced as voiceless unaspirated [p, t] (Coetzee et al. 2018). [...] the phonetic cues to obstruent voicing are allowing tone to emerge in a process of tonogenesis, where phonological tone arises in a previously non-tonal language (Hombert 1975). [...] What was a historical obstruent voicing contrast is now variably produced, and with a strengthened f0 cue; this suggests that this is a case of tonogenesis, where the secondary f0 cues of the original obstruent voicing contrast are being rephonologized as tone.
sources.locator: p. 270, section 1 Introduction and p. 284, section 5 Conclusion
sources.note: First-hand production (VOT, f0 at 11 points) and perception (VOT x f0 continua) study of word-initial /b d/ vs /p t/ across age and gender groups: the historical voicing contrast is variably neutralised (devoicing) while a strengthened f0 difference on the following vowel (low after historically voiced, high after voiceless) carries the contrast; interpreted as ongoing tonogenesis (f0 cues rephonologised as tone in a previously non-tonal language), led by female speakers of all ages; listeners weight f0 more for female voices. sources.note: Incipient tonogenesis: voiced plosives are losing prevoicing while the following vowel keeps a 50-100 Hz lower F0, so pitch is coming to carry the old voicing contrast; no tone inventory is proposed.

tone.quote: This devoicing is nearly categorical: VOTs of devoiced plosives average 12 ms and those of phonologically voiceless plosives average 17 ms. … The contrast appears to be preserved in the F0 contour of the following vowel, which is 50 to 100 Hz lower (depending on the speaker) after phonologically voiced than after phonologically voiceless plosives. The F0 difference continues through at least 70% of the vowel. However, post-plosive F0 variation is not contingent on devoicing, e.g., F0 contours after phonological /b/ are the same regardless of whether the production is [p] or [b].
